output.situation: You are currently paralyzed by the search for a 'calling' while weighing the practical need for security against a desire for meaningful connection. The central tension lies in whether your purpose is something to be discovered as a static identity or constructed through your current actions and commitments.

minds.title: The Existentialist
minds.concern: The radical freedom to define one's own essence.
minds.author: Jean-Paul Sartre

minds.title: The Pragmatist
minds.concern: The practical calculation of utility and well-being.
minds.author: John Stuart Mill

minds.title: The Stoic
minds.concern: The alignment of individual action with duty and nature.
minds.author: Marcus Aurelius

debate.speaker: The Existentialist
debate.text: You are waiting for a 'calling' as if it were a pre-written script. But existence precedes essence. You do not discover a purpose; you create it by the choices you make every day.
debate.author: Jean-Paul Sartre

debate.speaker: The Pragmatist
debate.text: That is a high-stakes burden. Before you try to invent your essence, consider that stability is a necessary precursor to happiness. You need a foundation of security to actually enjoy time with those you love.
debate.author: John Stuart Mill

debate.speaker: The Stoic
debate.text: Stability is not found in external circumstances, but in how you perform your role. You are a part of a greater whole; your 'calling' is simply to act well in the situation you are currently in.
debate.author: Marcus Aurelius

debate.speaker: The Existentialist
debate.text: Acting well in a situation is fine, but it risks becoming a passive acceptance of your environment. You must choose your projects, not just endure your duties, or you will never feel authentic.
debate.author: Jean-Paul Sartre

debate.speaker: The Pragmatist
debate.text: I disagree that it is passive. If you choose a path that provides stability, you are maximizing your capacity to contribute to others. That is a rational way to judge the value of your choices.
debate.author: John Stuart Mill

debate.speaker: The Stoic
debate.text: But if you focus only on the utility of your choices, you will always be anxious about the outcome. If you focus on the integrity of your actions, you find peace, regardless of how your life looks to others.
debate.author: Marcus Aurelius

debate.speaker: The Existentialist
debate.text: I see the value in that focus, but only if you acknowledge that you are the one deciding what 'integrity' means. I revise my position: integrity is not a standard, it's a commitment you sustain.
debate.author: Jean-Paul Sartre

debate.speaker: The Pragmatist
debate.text: That commitment makes sense if it allows for the flourishing of your relationships. Perhaps stability isn't the opposite of a calling; it's the infrastructure that lets you pursue one without crashing.
debate.author: John Stuart Mill

debate.speaker: The Stoic
debate.text: Then we agree: you do not need to wait for a 'calling.' You need only to commit to your current responsibilities and treat your daily actions as the only project that truly belongs to you.
debate.author: Marcus Aurelius

output.clearer: The main insight is that your 'calling' is likely not a hidden treasure but a byproduct of how you engage with your current responsibilities. The dispute remains over whether you should prioritize the pursuit of a specific project (Existentialism) or find meaning by fulfilling your duties within a stable life (Stoicism and Pragmatism). You might reflect on whether your anxiety about a calling is actually a fear of committing to one thing at the expense of others.
output.dependsOn: If your primary goal is to minimize regret for not 'trying,' prioritize small, experimental projects alongside your stable work. If your goal is to minimize anxiety about your future, focus on the immediate duties and relationships in your present environment. If you remain uncertain about what you value, test your assumptions by committing to a low-stakes, short-term project to see if the 'calling' you seek is found in the doing rather than the choosing.
